title: STEM Investigation of Structural and Chemical Stability of Na-Ion Cathode Materials
content: Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) offer a sustainable alternative to lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) amid supply and environmental concerns [1, 2]. The cathode, responsible for over 60% efficiency, requires structural stability and open ion pathways for higher energy density [3]. However, atomistic characterization is needed to understand degradation mechanisms. Our study finds a long plateau at 4.18 V, indicating a P2–O2 phase transition that accelerates capacity fade during cycling (Fig. 1a) which is identical with a previous study [4]. In the literature [5], it is recommended that Ni oxidation primarily occurs below 4.0 V, driving phase changes Oxygen. K-edge spectra reveal stronger bulk oxidation than at the surface, with pre-edge peaks indicating Ni and lattice oxygen oxidation. A recent work [6] shows that A 1.62° (002) peak shift in Na2/3Ni₁/3Mn2/3O2 (NNMO) at full charge suggests increased O-type stacking faults, leading to volume changes and structural degradation. Beyond 4.2 V, NNMO undergoes a clear P2–O2 transition, where lattice mismatch induces stress and capacity decay.
